## Introduction and Scope

Useful intelligence will not scale forever through one context window, one memory state, and one serial reasoning path. At some point, serious work must branch. Different attempts must inspect different evidence, use different tools, preserve different memories, edit different artifacts, test different hypotheses, and check one another's results. In this sense, multi-agent LLM systems are not a curiosity. They are the natural form of scaled test-time computation.

But inevitability is not reliability. Extra agents do not automatically create intelligence. They create more work, more messages, more state, more artifacts, and more ways for errors to spread. The central question is therefore how, not whether: what machinery turns divided computation into reliable, useful work?

Human society is the clearest existence proof that intelligence can scale through divided labor. It is also the clearest warning. Society does not scale because people merely talk to one another. It scales through records, tools, roles, rules, markets, tests, review, and institutions that let separate work accumulate. Multi-agent LLM systems face the same basic problem in a new medium: independent work must be routed, checked, selected, merged, remembered, or rejected.

The 2023 wave bet that LLMs could shortcut the coordination problem. If one language model can already imitate a planner, programmer, critic, or reviewer, perhaps prompting several models into role-specialized workers would produce useful division of labor without engineering the coordination machinery that human organizations required. The single-agent ingredients were already available: ReAct-style reasoning-action loops had shown that an LLM could plan, act, and observe in sequence [@react]. The multi-agent branch began when those loops were multiplied into separately stateful workers whose outputs had to be routed, checked, selected, or merged.

The early wave converted the abstract idea of multiple LLM calls into recognizable coordination forms. CAMEL and Generative Agents made role play, memory, reflection, and social simulation vivid [@camel; @generativeagents]. ChatDev and MetaGPT mapped software work onto company-like stages [@chatdev; @metagpt]. AutoGen turned multi-agent interaction into programmable conversations among LLMs, tools, code execution, and humans [@autogen]. AgentVerse and AutoAgents studied recruitment and automatic team construction, while debate systems tested whether multiple speakers or judges could critique, aggregate, and refine answers [@agentverse; @autoagents; @du2023debate; @multiagentdebate; @chateval]. Survey work has mapped this expanding ecosystem, but the field now also needs a historical synthesis of how the evidence changed [@llmmultagentsurvey].

The organization image was productive because it gave the field a language for dividing work. Agent teams could be described in terms familiar from human work: manager, engineer, reviewer, tester, scientist, judge, memory manager, tool user, and specialist. It also made coordination concrete. A multi-agent system was no longer just a prompt. It was a choice about who acts, who sees what, who can use which tools, what state is saved, what evidence is checked, and when the process stops.

The image was also incomplete. It encouraged the assumption that social structure itself creates capability. The 2024-2026 evidence forced a sharper view. Realistic benchmarks show that LLM agents are brittle in browsers, operating systems, codebases, APIs, games, and long-horizon tool-use environments [@agentbench; @agentboard; @webarena; @visualwebarena; @osworld; @gaia; @workarena; @browsergym; @androidworld; @taubench; @swebench; @agentcompany]. Cost-aware evaluation warns that more model calls are not the same thing as better agent design [@aiagentsmatter]. Failure taxonomies show that multi-agent errors often arise from system design, inter-agent misalignment, and weak task verification, not only from isolated model mistakes [@whymultiagentfail].

The lesson is not that multi-agent systems are a dead end. It is the opposite. If multi-agent systems are the route from isolated model responses to organized AI work, then the field must stop mistaking agent count for mechanism. Equal-budget controls show that a single agent with the same thinking-token budget can outperform multi-agent variants on some multi-hop reasoning tasks [@singleagentoutperforms]. Collaboration and long-horizon artifact benchmarks show that delegation, communication, and repeated editing can degrade work even when local outputs look plausible [@cooperbench; @delegate52; @slopcodebench]. More agents help only when they add useful search, useful memory, useful tools, useful critique, useful branches, or useful checks.

The durable thesis is therefore:

> Multi-agent LLM systems are the route by which LLMs scale from isolated responses to organized work. Their central scientific and engineering problem is coordination: how to turn many separately stateful attempts into evidence, artifacts, and decisions that survive verification.

That thesis determines the scope. This review uses **multi-agent LLM system** broadly: a system in which multiple model-backed, tool-backed, or human-backed workers maintain separate state, prompts, roles, tools, memories, action histories, or artifact branches while contributing to one task or workflow. The minimum unit is a separately controlled trajectory: a worker with its own context, interface, or work product whose output must later be selected, routed, checked, or merged. The agents may converse directly, route artifacts through an orchestrator, vote independently, edit isolated branches, or share a memory store. This definition includes role-playing chat systems, software-agent teams, debate and judging panels, mixture-of-agent aggregators, multi-agent research systems, and generalist agent platforms. Human-backed workers are included only when they participate in an LLM-mediated workflow whose model or tool outputs require coordination. Ordinary single-agent chain-of-thought prompting is excluded unless multiple workers or separately controlled attempts are part of the coordination problem.

The definition is functional rather than anthropomorphic. In LLM systems, an "agent" may be a role prompt, a controller loop, a tool-using process, a memory manager, a reviewer, a branch worker, a judge, or a human proxy. What matters is not whether the worker resembles a person. What matters is whether the system splits work into separately stateful attempts and then coordinates the resulting evidence, state, or artifacts so a human or verifier can decide what survives.

This makes agent count a weak descriptor. A system with many agents may only be spending more tokens, sampling more answers, or laundering one bad premise through a longer transcript. A smaller system may create real multi-agent value if it partitions evidence, tools, memories, critiques, artifact branches, or human judgment in a way that can be checked. The causal question is what the split made possible. Did it create independent attempts, expose different evidence, improve criticism, isolate artifact work, preserve useful state, route work better, or use human judgment more effectively? Each answer implies a different baseline: more serial reasoning, more samples, better prompts, stronger models, better tools, or a stronger final verifier.

The history of the field is a movement toward that distinction. Early work made artificial organizations vivid; later benchmarks and controls made coordination costs visible; the emerging synthesis asks what kind of divided work survives verification. @tbl-history-phases summarizes that movement, and @fig-history shows the same arc as a compact timeline.

| Period | Dominant question | Representative systems and evaluations | Main lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-LLM and adjacent foundations | What did earlier coordination and tool-use work fail to provide? | MAS, MARL, emergent communication, ReAct, tool-use agents, early agent benchmarks | MARL warned that agents do not coordinate automatically, but modern LLM multi-agent systems required a new substrate: agent harnesses, tools, memory, artifacts, and test-time orchestration. |
| 2023 agent societies | Can LLM roles, memory, and conversation produce useful collective behavior? | CAMEL, Generative Agents, ChatDev, MetaGPT, AutoGen, AgentVerse, AutoAgents, debate systems | Role play made decomposition and orchestration concrete, but often confounded collaboration with more inference and selection. |
| 2023-2025 agent evaluation | Can tool-using agents complete realistic tasks? | WebArena, VisualWebArena, OSWorld, GAIA, AgentBench, WorkArena, tau-bench, SWE-bench | Fluent interaction was far ahead of reliable task completion; benchmarks shifted attention to state, tools, recovery, and verification. |
| 2024-2026 skeptical controls | When do multiple agents beat strong alternatives? | *AI Agents That Matter*, *Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?*, *Science of Scaling*, *Single-Agent Outperforms*, CooperBench, DELEGATE-52, SlopCodeBench | Gains must survive cost accounting, equal budgets, strong single-agent and sampling baselines, repeated trials, and degradation tests. |
| Emerging synthesis | How should work be allocated, checked, trained, merged, and escalated under limited human supervision? | CAID, MemMA, AgentRxiv, AI co-scientist, Magentic-One, GPTSwarm, MaAS, OMAC, AgentNet, MAPoRL, MASLab | The durable architecture keeps separate work inspectable, verified, mergeable, and governed by humans where judgment matters. |

: Historical phases in modern multi-agent LLM systems, from pre-LLM coordination foundations to artifact-centered and optimized orchestration. Each phase changed the evidence standard for claims about when multiple agents help. {#tbl-history-phases}
